CHAPTER 01 | Nutrition ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 10 In 400 BC, the Greek physician Hippocrates declared, “Let thy food be thy medicine and thy medicine be thy food.” The ancient “father of medicine” had begun to realize a person’s health is greatly impacted by their food, and it could be used to prevent disease and maintain wellness. Over time, simple observations have led to many scientific discoveries and declarations regarding nutrition, nutrients, and how the body turns food on a plate into energy for life. In 1747, Dr. James Lind of the British Navy discovered scurvy in sailors who were only fed bread and meat. His experiments with items such as salt water, citrus fruit, and vinegar allowed him to find evidence that citrus prevented the disease even though vitamin C wasn’t discovered until 1912 and not chemically produced until the 1930s. Figure 1.1 Dutch Sailors Died of Scurvy Illustrated in the Le Tour de Monde Travel Journal (1865) In the 1770s, Antoine Lavoisier used his knowledge of chemistry to develop the concept of the body’s metabolism without knowledge of elements such as carbon, nitrogen, and hydrogen, which weren’t discovered until the 1800s. Vitamins and their importance in health and wellness were discovered in the early 1900s by European doctors. The research and scientific discoveries in the field of dietetics and nutrition continue to this day. With the introduction of the nutrition field in the late 19th century, nutrition experts have been employed in hospitals to monitor troops, schools to ensure balanced meals for youth, and as a major aspect of the fitness and general health industries.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 11 Pursuing the education needed to successfully coach clients for health and fitness goals and improve overall well-being requires attention to detail and discussion of many topics. As awareness of how nutrition affects the health of each individual grows, the economic and demographic status, life stage, and energy requirements must all be considered. Topics like human energy systems, the digestive system, metabolism, and the human cell are critical for a nutrition coach to understand. HOW HUMANS SELECT FOOD The appeal of food goes beyond the need for energy and nutrients. Humans select food based on their senses: sight, smell, taste, and feel. SIGHT The eyes provide the first impression of food, such as the shape, color, shine, texture, size, and presence of defects. A human can discern information from what they see, like how ripe a fruit is or if it has been heated or burned. The color of foods contributes to their appeal to the consumer as well. SMELL The human olfactory system can discern between 2,000 and 4,000 different smells, with highly sensitive people being able to distinguish up to 10,000 different odors. The nose detects the volatile molecules of foods, which are generated from the application of heat. Therefore, it is far easier to smell warm foods than cold ones. TASTE When consuming food, taste is typically the most influential sense. The taste buds in the mouth are arranged on the tongue but are also found in the palate and in the pharynx. The addition of saliva to food makes it possible to taste, and this sense is a combination of smell and taste (volatile and nonvolatile compounds). Every human has between 9,000 and 10,000 taste buds, but they diminish over time. As humans age, they can still taste just fine but may find themselves using far more seasonings on their foods. Through taste, humans can discern bitter, sour, sweet, salty, and umami (savory). OLFACTORY SYSTEM: The organ system used for smelling. VOLATILE MOLECULES: Small, vaporized particles. TASTE: The perception stimulated when a substance in the mouth reacts chemically with a taste receptor cell in the oral cavity. UMAMI: One of the five categories of taste in food, corresponding to the flavor of glutamates, especially monosodium glutamate.

CHAPTER 01 | Nutrition ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 12 FEEL Texture (how foods feel to the hands as people handle them) and mouthfeel as they consume it drive the way humans select foods. While this sensation is unique for everyone, texture can affect the way the brain processes the taste and smell of a food. For example, if someone does not like the texture of a tomato, it may taste “bad” to them. However, the texture of tomato paste (which is simply pureed tomato) may not bother them, and this taste is palatable. The consistency of food describes its firmness or thickness and goes hand in hand with food texture. FLAVOR Flavor is not a sensory tool used by humans but a combination of taste, smell, and mouthfeel. This explains why a stuffy nose makes food taste very different than when the sinuses are clear. Flavor is a very important factor determining the success or failure of food items (processed and fresh) in the consumer marketplace. Flavor is heavily influenced by the amount of fat in the food. This explains why reduced fat or fat-free products do not taste quite the same as their full fat counterparts. However, the addition of other compounds like sugar or sweeteners to lower fat foods may make them taste sweeter. FUNCTIONAL FOODS Foods for a specified health use are referred to as functional foods. Functional foods are those selected, produced, or consumed for reasons beyond calorie and nutrient content. This term was coined in Japan, where the functional food market is one of the most advanced in the world. Functional foods are divided into four categories: modified foods, conventional foods, medical foods, and special dietary foods. MODIFIED FOODS Modified foods are foods modified through enhancement, enrichment, or nutrient fortification. This can include calcium-fortified juice, folate-enriched breads, and beverages enhanced with energy-promoting substances like caffeine and vitamin B complex. CONVENTIONAL FOODS Conventional foods are simple, unmodified whole foods like vegetables and fruits. These foods have been linked to reduced cancer and chronic disease risk, heart health, and urinary tract function. Examples include broccoli, tomatoes, and kale. MOUTHFEEL: The physical sensations in the mouth caused by food or drink. PALATABLE: Pleasant to taste. CONSISTENCY: The firmness or thickness of a food. FLAVOR: A combination of taste, smell, and mouthfeel. FUNCTIONAL FOODS: Foods selected, produced, or consumed for reasons beyond calorie and nutrient content. MODIFIED FOODS: Foods modified through enhancement, enrichment, or nutrient fortification. CONVENTIONAL FOODS: Simple, unmodified whole foods like vegetables and fruits.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 13 MEDICAL FOODS Medical foods are defined as foods intended to be ingested under the supervision of a physician for specific dietary management of a disease or condition. Examples include canned or bottled supplements for the treatment of diabetes or liver disease. SPECIALTY DIETARY FOODS Specialty dietary foods are defined by the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act with three distinctions: 1 They support a dietary need from a physiological, physical, or pathological condition. 2 They supply vitamins, minerals, or other ingredients with the intent of increasing intake. 3 They support a dietary need by being a sole item in a diet (lactose free, gluten free, or similar). THE SOCIAL DETERMINANTS OF HEALTH AND NUTRITION The social determinants of health are the non-medical factors that influence a person’s overall well-being, including their nutrition habits and behaviors. These determinants include income level, education, access to healthcare, social support, and the physical environments in which people live and work. When it comes to food choices, these social influences often dictate what, how much, and how often individuals can eat, directly impacting their nutritional status and long-term health outcomes. For example, individuals living in low-income neighborhoods may experience limited access to fresh, whole foods due to a lack of nearby grocery stores or farmers’ markets. These areas are often referred to as food deserts. Without affordable or convenient access to nutritious options, people may rely on highly processed foods from convenience stores or fast-food restaurants. These foods are often high in sugar, fat, and sodium, but low in essential vitamins and minerals. Over time, these eating patterns can contribute to chronic conditions such as obesity, diabetes, and heart disease. Education also plays a critical role in nutritional decision-making. People with limited education may not receive the same exposure to basic health literacy or nutrition information, making it difficult to interpret food labels, understand dietary guidelines, or make informed food choices. Individuals with higher education levels are more likely to be employed in jobs that offer health benefits, flexible schedules, or wellness programs—resources that can support healthy eating habits. MEDICAL FOODS: Food intended to be ingested under the supervision of a physician for specific dietary management of a disease or condition. FOOD DESERTS: Urban areas where it is difficult to afford or find quality whole foods. SPECIALTY DIETARY FOODS: Foods supporting a condition, supplying vitamins or minerals to increase intake, or serving as the sole item in a diet.

CHAPTER 01 | Nutrition ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 14 Social environments and culture shape nutrition behavior as well. Cultural traditions, religious beliefs, and social norms influence food preferences, preparation methods, and the timing of meals. Social support systems, such as family and community networks, can either reinforce or challenge nutritional behaviors. For example, individuals surrounded by peers who value healthy eating may be more likely to adopt similar habits. Those in socially isolated environments may lack the encouragement or accountability needed to maintain consistent nutrition practices. Recognizing and addressing these social determinants is essential for creating equitable access to nutritious food and improving overall health in diverse populations. CULTURAL CONSIDERATIONS Culture describes the ideas, customs, skills, and art of a group of people in a period of civilization. Many cultures exist, including American culture. The Papuan people of Papua New Guinea, the Gauchos of South America, and the San people of Botswana are also examples of the many cultures around the world. In some cultures, food is prized, and in others, it is spurned. Whale blubber is a staple in arctic areas, and dog is considered a delicacy in parts of Asia. Grubs are consumed for protein in Australia, escargot (snails) are popular in France, and sushi is an Asian staple becoming more popular across the globe. Figure 1.2 San Bushmen of Mariental, Namibia Ethnicity and Place of Birth The ethnic origins of an individual and their place of birth will determine what foods they are exposed to. Nearly 25 percent of the American population are ethnic minorities or were born in another country before coming to the United States. The foods that are commonplace or CULTURE: The ideas, customs, skills, and art of a group of people in a period of civilization.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 15 influenced by their cultures have traveled to the United States with them, and foods like pizza, Thai, Moroccan, and Vietnamese cuisine are more common. Figure 1.3 Ethnic Foods Can be Found in Most Cities. Cultural competence is an essential skill for nutrition coaches working with diverse populations. Each client brings a unique set of beliefs, traditions, and preferences that influence their relationship with food. Being aware of these factors helps coaches build trust, improve communication, and tailor nutrition guidance in ways that respect individual backgrounds. A one-size-fits-all approach is rarely effective—coaches must be willing to listen, learn, and adapt their strategies to meet clients where they are. Understanding cultural influences on food selection, meal timing, fasting practices, and even views on body image allows coaches to offer relevant, realistic recommendations. This sensitivity also helps avoid inadvertently reinforcing stereotypes or making assumptions that could damage the coaching relationship. By creating an inclusive and respectful environment, nutrition coaches are better equipped to support long-term behavior change and empower clients to make sustainable choices that align with both their health goals and cultural values. ECONOMIC CONSIDERATIONS The availability of food can change based on the local economic status of a city or neighborhood. Many Americans live in food deserts—urban areas where fresh fruits, vegetables, and meats are not readily available. In these areas, consumers rely on processed foods from convenience stores and markets.

CHAPTER 01 | Nutrition ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 16 Figure 1.4 Markets Are Common, but Not Everywhere When fresh, whole foods are available, they may be financially out of reach. The cost of fresh fruits is generally higher than the cost of processed, sugary foods, and families and individuals with income restrictions will often forgo the healthy options for the less expensive, unhealthy ones. Government assistance programs are becoming more widely available to reduce the cost of whole foods and supply extra funds dedicated to groceries for individuals and families in need. Again, economic empathy is a critical aspect of effective nutrition coaching. Understanding that clients may face financial constraints impacting their access to nutritious foods allows coaches to offer realistic, judgment-free guidance. Not every client has the resources to purchase organic produce, specialty items, or supplements, and assuming otherwise can create unnecessary pressure or guilt. Coaches who demonstrate empathy and flexibility can help clients build healthy eating habits within their means—prioritizing budget-friendly, nutrient-dense options and offering creative solutions for meal planning and preparation. When nutrition coaches approach conversations with awareness and compassion for a client’s financial situation, they create a more supportive and sustainable coaching experience. This might include recommending frozen or canned vegetables, bulk pantry staples, or affordable protein sources, while still addressing the client’s goals. By meeting clients where they are, nutrition coaches can encourage consistency and confidence, reinforcing that healthy eating is achievable without requiring perfection or privilege.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 17 RELIGIOUS CONSIDERATIONS Religious competence is important for nutrition coaches who aim to support clients with integrity and respect. Many religions include specific dietary practices, food preparation guidelines, and fasting periods that directly affect a client’s eating habits and availability of certain foods. A coach who is informed and sensitive to these practices can better align nutrition recommendations with the client’s values, avoiding conflicts that may hinder adherence or comfort. This awareness not only promotes inclusivity but also strengthens the coach-client relationship through a foundation of understanding and trust. One example includes Buddhists who consider it uncompassionate to eat the flesh of another living creature, and many, though not all, are vegetarians. Hindus do not believe in injuring or killing an animal for its meat. Cows are sacred in that culture. Thus, the devout Hindu diet rejects poultry, eggs, and meats. Figure 1.5 A Jewish Holiday Meal The Mormon church discourages parishioners from drinking coffee, alcohol, and tea. In the Orthodox Jewish faith, the consumption of kosher foods. Kosher foods include ruminant animals (sheep, cows, and goats), chicken, goose, fruits, and vegetables. The allowed animals are considered kosher if their slaughter is supervised by a rabbi or authorized individual to ensure the blood is removed properly. Similarly, halal foods are permitted foods in Islam. Halal foods do not allow animal blood, improper slaughter, intoxicants, or decay. KOSHER: Foods “fit” for consumption per the requirements of Jewish law. HALAL FOODS: Foods deemed “acceptable” for consumption by Muslim law.

Practices vary widely. “Are there any religious or seasonal traditions that affect how or when you eat throughout the year?” Roman Catholic Fasting or abstaining from meat on Fridays during Lent, holiday feasts, emphasis on moderation. “Do any religious observances influence your food choices or meal timing, especially around certain holidays?” Judaism Kosher dietary laws (no pork or shellfish, separation of dairy and meat, specific slaughter requirements), fasting on Yom Kippur, Passover restrictions. “Do you follow kosher guidelines, and are there any food rules or traditions I should be aware of when helping you plan meals?” Islam Halal food requirements, no pork or alcohol, fasting during Ramadan (no food or drink from sunrise to sunset). “Do you observe halal dietary practices or participate in fasting like Ramadan? How can I support you during those times?”

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 19 Table 1.1 Common Religious and Cultural Groups and Considerations Hinduism Many Hindus are vegetarian; avoid beef; may fast on certain days; food is often linked with purity. “Are there any foods you avoid for religious reasons or days when you typically fast or change your eating habits?” Buddhism Many practice vegetarianism or veganism; fasting or mindful eating may be common depending on the sect. “Do you follow any specific dietary practices or eating styles that are part of your spiritual practice?” Seventh-day Adventist Emphasis on plant-based diets, no alcohol, tobacco, or caffeine; some avoid meat entirely. “Are there any foods or substances you avoid for faith-based reasons that I should keep in mind?” Eastern Orthodox Christianity Fasting periods throughout the year; may avoid meat, dairy, and eggs on fast days. “Do you observe any fasting periods or food restrictions during certain times of the year?” Native American/ Indigenous Traditional diets vary by tribe; importance placed on natural, seasonal, or sacred foods; often disrupted by modern access and affordability issues. “Are there traditional foods or practices that are important to your culture or personal health that we can include in your plan?” Asian Cultural Traditions (e.g., Chinese, Japanese) Importance of food balance (e.g., yin/yang), rice as a staple, hot vs. cold foods, symbolic foods during holidays. “Are there any cultural food practices or ingredients that are especially important to you or your family?”
